sources.title: Eclipse S-CORE
sources.role: Pinned official project-page snapshot used to verify platform scope, layering, code-first orientation and current stated release-gate status.

claims.text: The S-CORE project page states that it targets software-platform layers above the SoC board-support package and below the application layer, spanning OS abstraction, middleware and application-level services.
The page explicitly describes S-CORE as code-first, with executable code, tests, CI and reference implementations rather than only a paper standard.
The page identifies hardware/software decoupling, modularity and project-specific extensibility as platform goals.
The pinned page snapshot states that S-CORE had reached release gate v0.8 and describes stronger requirements/architecture/safety-artifact expectations for modules in scope for v1.0.
claims.context: Direct page content at the pinned observation time; not equivalent to safety certification.

limitations.text: Statements such as 'production-ready' or predictable/safe behavior are project claims unless backed by separate certification, conformance or deployment evidence.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on eclipse-score-project; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The pinned project page provides direct evidence of S-CORE's intended stack boundaries, code-first delivery model and current project-status language; safety/production claims remain project claims.

editorial.why_now_note: S-CORE is a concrete shared runtime/platform effort that directly reflects the shift from proprietary per-OEM core stacks toward common automotive software infrastructure.
editorial.rationale: Strong platform-level candidate when combined with release-series evidence and explicit maturity caveats.

sources.title: The Eclipse Foundation Launches the S-CORE Project
sources.role: Official Eclipse Foundation launch announcement used for project intent, layer placement, supporters and stated safety-development direction.

claims.text: The Eclipse Foundation describes S-CORE as core software commonly called middleware, positioned between the operating system and application layer.
claims.context: Project positioning in the launch announcement.

claims.text: The announcement frames S-CORE as an open-source common core stack for software-defined vehicles intended to reduce duplicated non-differentiating platform work.
claims.context: Foundation/project rationale rather than measured industry outcome.

claims.text: The announcement states that the S-CORE development process was under audit by a certification agency and aimed to support production of open-source software suitable for safety-critical standards such as ISO 26262.
claims.context: Status/goal as announced in June 2025; not certification evidence.

limitations.text: The announcement included forward-looking release targets and safety-process goals; those targets are not treated here as proof of later delivery or certification.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on eclipse-score-launch; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The official launch announcement verifies the June 2025 project launch context and stated platform/safety goals while keeping forward-looking claims distinct from later release evidence.

editorial.why_now_note: The launch marks an industry collaboration moving from interface specifications toward shared code for the SDV core stack.
editorial.rationale: Architecture-significant ecosystem event, best read together with the S-CORE project page and release-series Evidence rather than as standalone maturity proof.

sources.title: SOAFEE Blueprint: DENSO develops deterministic middleware for SDV
sources.role: SOAFEE-hosted DENSO-authored blueprint used for deterministic middleware architecture, mixed-criticality goals and demonstration framing.

claims.text: DENSO describes using the open-source Lingua Franca time-coordination language to define application behavior and support time-centric scheduling/runtime monitoring.
claims.context: DENSO-authored architecture claim hosted as a SOAFEE blueprint.

claims.text: The blueprint proposes running safety and non-safety workloads in parallel while combining cloud-native technologies with functional-safety and real-time requirements, including application-level safety envelopes and violation detection.
The article states that the first blueprint demonstrates the approach using an Autoware Foundation automated-driving stack.

limitations.text: The page is authored by DENSO and hosted by SOAFEE; deterministic guarantees and portability/safety benefits are vendor/project claims rather than independent certification evidence.
The pinned article does not provide a sufficiently detailed independent latency/jitter or safety-certification evaluation for quantitative comparison.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on soafee-denso-deterministic-middleware; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The blueprint directly verifies the proposed time-centric/mixed-criticality middleware architecture and demonstration framing; its guarantees remain VENDOR_CLAIM.

editorial.why_now_note: The blueprint is a useful industry implementation pattern connecting cloud-native SDV development to deterministic mixed-critical execution.
editorial.rationale: Strong architecture signal if presented explicitly as a DENSO/SOAFEE blueprint rather than neutral proof of deterministic performance.

sources.title: An Investigation of the AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform from an Industry Perspective
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors use Design Science Research and build a minimal AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform as an experimental prototype to investigate application-development pain points.
They report that pain points arise from a combination of AUTOSAR specification-inherent choices, vendor implementation and local organizational practices.
The authors identify configuration-file management and developer understanding/training around the Adaptive application runtime life cycle as areas requiring better tooling/support.

limitations.text: The accessible primary abstract does not expose the minimal-AP implementation scope, participant/industry context, concrete pain-point inventory, trace from each pain point to specification/vendor/local causes, or study validity discussion.
Findings explicitly mix specification, vendor implementation and local practice; they should not be generalized as intrinsic AUTOSAR Adaptive defects without item-level attribution.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for An Investigation of the AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform from an Industry Perspective; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The primary abstract verifies the Design Science/minimal-AP method and three-way pain-point attribution, but detailed prototype/study evidence and validity limits remain unresolved.

unresolved_questions: Inspect the full paper for minimal-AP components, industry context, detailed pain-point taxonomy, attribution evidence and threats to validity.

editorial.why_now_note: AUTOSAR Adaptive is a key service/runtime layer for central HPCs; implementation and configuration friction materially affects whether the architectural standard translates into deployable SDV software.
editorial.rationale: High-value candidate because it examines specification-versus-implementation-versus-local causes, but exact pain-point attribution requires full-paper inspection.
